summary: Pupils (age 8-9) convert between units of the same attribute: 3 km = 3000 m, 2 hours = 120 minutes, 5 weeks = 35 days. The organising principle is the inverse relationship between unit size and count — the smaller the unit, the more of them you need — so moving from a larger unit to a smaller one multiplies and the number gets bigger. Metric conversion builds on base-ten place value (kilo = 1000), but time runs in 60s and 7s and must not be forced into powers of ten. Compound measures (2 m 30 cm) must be converted to a common unit before combining.
misconceptions: Converts in the wrong direction — divides when the larger→smaller move should multiply, or expects the smaller-unit answer to be a smaller number
Treats a compound measure like 2 m 30 cm as one number (230, or 2.30) instead of converting and adding
Over-applies base-ten to time — an hour becomes 100 minutes
Doesn't securely know the relationship (uses 100 cm in a km, 30 days in a week)

activities.title: One length, two scales: seeing why larger→smaller multiplies
steps: Look at one physical length laid against two scales stacked together — e.g. a metre scale and a centimetre scale — each with its own counter showing how many of that unit fit the length
Make the length longer and watch BOTH counts rise, then say which count rises faster and which is always the bigger number

Explain in your own words why the smaller unit always gives the bigger count (one large unit holds many small units, so the multiplier equals how many small units fit one large unit — e.g. 100 cm in a metre)

Feed a value through a '×/÷' gate to convert between a larger and a smaller unit and back; use the km↔m case where the factor is ×1000/÷1000 because 1 km = 1000 m, and note that a different pair has a different factor (100 for cm per m)
Deliberately pick the wrong gate once and describe why the answer is an absurd size (e.g. 3 km wrongly divided to 0.003 m)
State the rule you observed: larger unit → fewer, larger units; smaller unit → more units, so larger→smaller multiplies
activities.insight: Why larger→smaller multiplies: because a larger unit holds many of the smaller unit, the smaller-unit count is always the bigger number — the inverse relationship between unit size and count, observed rather than memorised. The exact multiplier depends on the pair (100 for cm↔m, 1000 for m↔km).

activities.title: Known-facts reference: metric vs time
steps: Build and keep a reference of the relationships as secure known facts: 1000 m = 1 km, 60 seconds = 1 minute, 60 minutes = 1 hour, 7 days = 1 week
Sort the facts into two groups — metric (base-ten, follows place value: kilo = 1000) and time (60s and 7s, NOT powers of ten)
Reveal the meaning of metric prefixes (e.g. kilo = 1000, centi = one hundredth) and tie each to a worked equivalent
Answer 'which is bigger, 90 cm or 1 m?' and explain how you know, so a bigger number does not fool you
Test yourself: 'How many minutes in 2 hours?' — then explain why the answer is 120, not 100
activities.insight: Correct conversion depends on knowing the right relationship securely, and on recognising that time is not base-ten; metric and time must be kept separate.

activities.title: Compound measures: convert before combining
steps: Write 2 m 30 cm all in centimetres: convert the metres first (2 m = 200 cm), then add the 30 cm to get 230 cm — explaining each step
Notice that adding the numbers across units (2 + 30 = 32) or writing 2.30 cm does NOT give the length; say why (2.30 m is a correct way to write it, but only with the metre unit)
Work a mixed set and check equivalences, e.g. decide true/false for '32 cm + 1.05 m = 150 cm − 0.13 m' by converting everything to one unit first
Combine two lengths given in different units, e.g. a '1.2 m' ribbon and a '90 cm' ribbon, by converting to a common unit before adding
activities.insight: A compound measure like 2 m 30 cm is not a single number; its parts must be converted to a common unit before they can be combined.

activities.title: Both-directions conversion practice targeting common errors
steps: Complete fill-in conversions in both directions: '3 km = ___ m' and '3000 m = ___ km'
Spot the wrong-direction answer, e.g. decide whether '3 km = 300 m' is right and correct it
Match equivalent measures across units and sort cards into groups of equal value
Convert 5 weeks to days and 2 hours to minutes, naming the factor used each time
Place a converted amount on a number line or tape diagram for a word problem
Explain, for one item, how you would reverse the conversion and why the operation changes (multiply ↔ divide as inverse operations)
activities.insight: Conversion is a two-way fluency procedure: multiply and divide are inverse operations, and direction is chosen by which unit is larger.

checkQuestion: Set a short mixed set of conversions and watch HOW the child works, not just the final numbers. (1) 'Convert 3 km into metres.' (2) 'How many minutes are there in 2 hours?' (3) 'Convert 5 weeks into days.' (4) 'A ribbon is 2 m 30 cm long. Write its length in centimetres.' Watch the direction of their operation, whether they use the right relationship, and how they treat the mixed units in (4).
checkAnswer: (1) 3 × 1000 = 3000 m — multiplies because a kilometre is the larger unit, so it holds many metres. (2) 2 × 60 = 120 min. (3) 5 × 7 = 35 days. (4) Converts the metres first — 2 m = 200 cm — then adds 30 cm to get 230 cm (not '2.30' or a strung-together '232'). Throughout, larger→smaller means multiply and the count gets bigger.
